idiom_name: validating NewX(...) (*X, error) constructor over unexported fields, or an unexported struct returned as an exported interface
implementation_notes: Go absorbs the Essence/CreationTarget split into package conventions instead of the classic two-class structure: the Essence role collapses into a package-level validating constructor func NewContract(customer, supplier string, start time.Time) (*Contract, error) that checks the compulsory properties with errors.New/fmt.Errorf and returns (nil, err) before any value escapes - validation before creation, and since Go has no constructor exceptions the error return is the only and therefore the idiomatic feedback channel. The restricted-constructor requirement is realized structurally: compulsory fields are unexported, so a cross-package composite literal like contract.Contract{...} cannot set them; the strongest form makes the whole struct type unexported and returns an exported interface from the constructor (the hash/crc32.New and adler32.New idiom documented in Effective Go), which leaves callers no way to name the type, so no Contract{}, var c Contract or new(Contract) exists outside the package. The classic Essence object is still justified for genuinely staged creation - many optional settings accumulated before one final validation, or interactive per-field feedback - where the Essence becomes a builder whose validateParameters() equivalent is a Validate() error method called before Build().
pitfalls: The zero value stays reachable even with all fields unexported: another package can declare var c contract.Contract or new(contract.Contract) and obtain an invalid instance (golang/go issue #333, declined) - either return an unexported struct type behind an exported interface so the type name is unrepresentable outside the package, or guard exported methods against the zero value.

Exported compulsory fields give no protection at all: any Contract{Customer: x} literal compiles and silently zeroes every omitted field, so compulsoriness must live in unexported fields plus the validating constructor, never in exported state.

Codecs construct without New: json.Unmarshal or a datastore loader into a fresh Contract cannot set unexported fields, so the instance silently stays at zero values instead of failing - deserialize into an intermediate form and pass it through the constructor, or revalidate at the load boundary.
Panicking on invalid compulsory properties fights the language: invalid input is an ordinary error, so return (nil, err) that callers can branch on; reserve panic for impossible programmer errors.
A nil *Contract after an ignored error: calling methods on the nil receiver crashes the program - never use the value when err != nil, and give methods a nil-receiver guard for defense in depth.
